name: Why Skeptics Are Ignored
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: The Asymmetry of Attention
lesson.summary: Skeptical arguments about quantum computing get far less media and institutional airtime than optimistic ones, not because they are weaker, but because of a predictable combination of incentive asymmetry and authority bias that shapes what gets amplified.
lesson.body:
Put the last two chapters together and a pattern emerges. Skeptics generally have little financial stake in the field's outcome, which makes their arguments worth taking seriously on the merits, while proponents often have substantial financial and career incentives tied to optimistic framing, which means their public statements deserve extra scrutiny. Given that pattern, a naive expectation might be that skeptical arguments would get roughly equal or even greater attention, precisely because they come from a more disinterested position. In practice, the opposite happens. Optimistic claims about quantum computing dominate media coverage, conference keynotes, and recruiting materials, while skeptical arguments circulate mostly within specialist circles. Understanding why requires looking past funding incentives to a second force: authority bias.

Authority bias is the tendency to give a claim more credibility because it comes from a prestigious source, independent of the strength of the argument itself. Quantum computing announcements tend to come from sources with enormous built in authority: major technology companies with famous brand names, well funded national laboratories, and government agencies making public investment announcements. A press release from a large, well known technology company attaching the word "breakthrough" to a new qubit result reaches millions of readers through the normal channels of business and technology journalism, often with limited scientific vetting along the way. A skeptical rebuttal published later, if it is published at all, typically appears in a much narrower venue: an academic blog, a specialist forum, a slower moving peer reviewed critique, and reaches a fraction of the audience.

There is also a structural asymmetry in how each side's claims are built. An optimistic claim about quantum computing's future often takes the form of a single, vivid announcement: a demonstration, a partnership, a funding round. It is easy to compress into a headline. A skeptical argument, by contrast, usually requires explaining several layers of technical nuance, why a demonstration was narrower than it sounded, why a benchmark problem was chosen for tractability rather than practical relevance, why coherence times at small scale do not simply extrapolate to large scale. Nuanced, multi step arguments are structurally harder to compress into shareable, attention grabbing content than a single confident announcement, regardless of which one is more accurate.

None of this means skeptics are always right and proponents are always wrong. It means the volume of attention each side receives is a poor proxy for the strength of their arguments, because attention is being generated by funding incentives and authority bias rather than by argument quality alone. A student trying to form an accurate picture of the field has to deliberately seek out the quieter, harder to find skeptical arguments rather than assuming that because they are less visible, they must be less credible. The imbalance in visibility is itself the thing to correct for, not a signal to trust.
